Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Game Presentation You are Ecomechanics: ‘New World’ artisans whose aim is to reduce the extraction of raw materials from our planet. Your art consists of constructing, repairing, or recycling pieces of robots that were the backbone of the labour force in the ‘old world’ of mass production, in order to transition from an extraction-based way of life to one that is more in tune with the physical limits of the planet. Your dream: To be honoured with the Ecomechanics’ most prestigious award: the Medal of the Order of the Leaf. Players are competing to get the most Recycling Points (RP). The one with the highest value at the end of the game wins.With 4 players, the game is played in teams, 2 vs. 2; teammates are sitting next to each other. Each player will score points individually, but the team's score is the lowest value of the two teammates. How the game is played Game setup Give one Shed to each Ecomechanic and place the following Parts inside them: 1 Nut, 1 Oil Drop, 1 Circuit Board, 2 Energy Place the correct number of randomly-drawn House Droid cards on the table. Create the deck(s) of droid cards according to the number of players. The cards are sorted by season and separated by an Interseason card Place the card distributor between the Ecomechanics Gameplay The game takes place over 3 rounds called Seasons, made up of a number of Turns. Turns A Turn is broken down into 3 phases, separated by optional phases: 1. Choose a Droid The Priority Ecomechanic draws one droid card per player from the deck, keeps one for themself and gives one to each other player 4 players: There is a Priority and a Secondary Echomecanic. They both draw 2 cards, keep one for themselves and give the other one to either their direct opponent or their teammate, depending on the turn. Optional: Swap Parts You have three ways to swap parts at the beginning of the game: Swap an Energy for a Base part (Nut, Oil drop or Circuit board) Swap 2 identical Base parts for any other Base part Swap 3 identical Base parts for an Energy 2. Action (1 of these 3): Repair: Discard the parts required on the bottom-left of the card to add the droid to your collection. Dismantle: Put the droid in the discard to gain the parts indicated on the upper-left of the card to add the droid to your collection. You are limited to 3 of each part (until you add Shed extensions), any excess part will be discarded. Construct: Put the droid in the discard and pay the parts required on bottom-left of a house card to add the house to your collection. You only have access to the house droids near you. 3. End of Turn If there are no more cards in the deck or an Ecomechanic does not have an available house droid, go to Game End If there is an Interseason card on the top of the deck: each player gains a Shed Extension, that allows to store one extra component of a given type in your Shed if a player has more leaves than their direct opponent(s), they gain a battery then discard the Interseason card If the game did not end, the next player becomes the Priority Mechanic, and you start a new turn. [Rating: 2/10] After 2 games on BGA: Cute illustrations, a likeable theme, but an extremely boring game. Within a very tight decision space, I have to make very annoying choices. Which of the two robots do I keep, which do I repair, or which do I dismantle? To make these decisions wisely, I have to check and compare resources. I find this annoying, exhausting, and not very rewarding. No exciting engine ever develops. I’m constantly looking at these little symbols; the story around them is completely irrelevant. [Rating: 4/10] Found it pretty uninteresting at two players. Maybe it would be better with more.

[Rating: 4/10] ok game. Rien à dire sur le fonctionnement, cela marche. Cependant, la partie ne m'a donné aucune sensation particulière.

[Rating: 4/10] You alternate handing out cards to your opponents. Resource conversion, somewhat opaque scoring. Pretty straightforward point salad. Beautiful art, but no new ground broken here. This is fine, but I dont see myself playing again.

[Rating: 4/10] Interesting take on you-split-I-choose but I'm not sure about when I'd put this on the  table over other options.

[Rating: 5/10] Draft cards, discard for resources or build (spending those same resources) for effects and points. We've seen it all before. The only novelty here is the draft: you draw one card for each player, may keep one and must give one to each other player. So you're constantly looking for "which card helps which opponent the least?" Which just feels too negative for me.  Not a bad game, but I didn't enjoy it.

[Rating: 5/10] What I like: - Play is simultaneous and the way turn order and card splitting is performed is interesting.  What I dislike: - Resource conversion, point salad, no meaningful interaction. I wasn't engaged and didn't really feel any tenseness in my decisions.

[Rating: 5/10] Super fast playing resource conversion game. Big fan of simultaneous actions, but there doesn't seem to be a lot of strategy/engine building here. You can't store resources or plan ahead, so it's seems like you repair droid until you can't pay for it, discard the next for resources, rinse, repeat. I think this might be best with 3 where you get to pick the best of 3 as the active player, and get to pick which card is worse for each of your 2 opponents.  It seems odd that the game ends when all 3 house droids are built - it's pretty easy for them to all get built half-way through the game.
